VALĀHAKAVAGGA. 103

1. There are these four types of clouds, monks. Which four? 
Thundering but not raining... <note>omission in text</note>... thundering and raining. 
These are the four types of clouds, monks.

2. In the same way, there are these four types of persons like clouds, monks, found existing in the world. Which four? 
Thundering but not raining... <note>omission in text</note>... thundering and raining.

3. And how, monks, is a person a thunderer but not a rainer? 
Here, monks, a certain person learns the <term>Dhamma</term> <gloss>teaching</gloss>: discourses, songs, expositions, verses, solemn utterances, sayings, birth stories, wonderful events, and answers to questions. But he does not understand as it really is: "This is suffering"... <note>omission in text</note>... "This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering." In this way, monks, a person is a thunderer but not a rainer; just as that cloud, monks, is a thunderer but not a rainer, so do I call this person.

4. And how, monks, is a person a rainer but not a thunderer? 
Here, monks, a certain person does not learn the <term>Dhamma</term> <gloss>teaching</gloss>: discourses... <note>omission in text</note>... answers to questions. But he understands as it really is: "This is suffering"... <note>omission in text</note>... "This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering." In this way, monks, a person is a rainer but not a thunderer; just as that cloud, monks, is... <note>omission in text</note>... I call this person.

5. And how, monks, is a person neither a thunderer nor a rainer? 
Here, monks, a certain person does not learn the <term>Dhamma</term> <gloss>teaching</gloss>: discourses... <note>omission in text</note>... answers to questions. And he does not understand as it really is: "This is suffering"... <note>omission in text</note>... "This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering." In this way, monks, a person is neither a thunderer nor a rainer; just as that cloud, monks, is... <note>omission in text</note>... I call this person.

6. And how, monks, is a person both a thunderer and a rainer? 
Here, monks, a certain person learns the <term>Dhamma</term> <gloss>teaching</gloss>: discourses... <note>omission in text</note>... answers to questions. And he understands as it really is: "This is suffering"... <note>omission in text</note>... "This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering." In this way, monks, a person is both a thunderer and a rainer; just as that cloud, monks, is both a thunderer and a rainer, so do I call this person.

<summary>This passage categorizes four types of individuals by comparing them to clouds based on their ability to study the teachings and their depth of insight into the Four Noble Truths.</summary>
<keywords>Cloud analogy, Dhamma, Four Noble Truths, suffering, monks, Buddhist pedagogy</keywords>
